stimuli.title: Streetlights and the Night Shift of Pollination
stimuli.body:
Ecologists have long known that artificial light draws moths away from their normal activities, but until recently the consequences were assumed to be minor. Moths are, after all, abundant, and the loss of a few individuals circling a lamp hardly seems to threaten an ecosystem. A recent field study of meadows suggests that this assumption was too casual. Researchers compared plots lit overnight by white LED lamps with matched plots left dark. In the lit plots, flower visits by moths fell by roughly 60 percent, and the plants there produced about a third fewer seeds than their counterparts in the dark, even though daytime visits by bees and hoverflies were the same in both kinds of plot.

The authors conclude that nocturnal pollinators perform a service that daytime insects cannot simply replace. Some plants open their flowers or release scent only after dusk, and for these species moths may be the main carriers of pollen.

Critics urge caution. The lit and dark plots were close together, so moths repelled from the lit plots may simply have moved to the dark ones, which would show a redistribution of visits rather than a loss. Moreover, seed production is not the same as population health: a plant that sets fewer seeds may still sustain itself if the surviving seedlings face less competition. The authors acknowledge both points but note that seed output in the dark plots did not rise above the regional norm, as a simple redistribution would predict. Whether night lighting harms plant populations over the long term remains to be tested.

stimuli.title: The Acquirer's Dilemma
stimuli.body:
Studies of corporate takeovers repeatedly find that, on average, the shareholders of acquiring firms gain little or lose value when a deal is announced, while those of the target firms gain handsomely. One popular explanation invokes the winner's curse. When several firms bid for a target whose true value is uncertain, each bidder forms its own estimate, some too high and some too low. The firm that wins is likely to be the one with the most optimistic estimate and therefore the one most likely to have overpaid. On this account, acquirers are no less competent than anyone else; the auction itself selects for error.

The winner's curse cannot, however, be the entire story. If it were, overpayment should be most severe in contested auctions and should largely disappear when a single bidder negotiates privately with a target, because a lone bidder has not been selected from a field of estimates. Yet the poor returns to acquirers are, if anything, only slightly less pronounced in uncontested deals. A second hypothesis, that executives systematically overestimate their own ability to extract value from the firms they buy, accounts for this pattern more comfortably, though it is harder to test, since hubris cannot be observed directly and is usually inferred from the very outcomes it is meant to explain. The most defensible view may be that both forces operate, with the winner's curse prominent in auctions and overconfidence everywhere.

stimuli.title: Cartels or Guarantors? The Medieval Guild Debate
stimuli.body:
For much of the twentieth century, historians of medieval and early modern Europe treated craft guilds as little more than cartels. By limiting the number of apprentices, fixing prices, and forbidding members to adopt new techniques, the argument ran, guilds protected the incomes of established masters at the expense of consumers and of would-be competitors, and in doing so slowed economic growth. This view echoed Adam Smith's complaint that people of the same trade seldom meet together without the conversation ending in a conspiracy against the public.

More recently, a group of economic historians has proposed a very different reading. In a world without brand names, product standards, or reliable courts, they argue, a buyer of cloth or of a silver cup had little means of judging its quality before purchase. Guilds addressed this problem. Long apprenticeships ensured that skills were passed on in a standard way; inspectors checked goods before they received the guild's mark; and members who cheated could be fined or expelled, so that the guild's collective reputation was worth protecting. Supporting evidence includes the observation that guild-stamped goods often fetched higher prices in distant markets, where buyers could not rely on personal acquaintance with the maker.

Neither account is entirely satisfactory, and it is a mistake to treat them as exclusive alternatives. The rules that certified quality were also, in practice, rules that limited entry: an apprenticeship long enough to guarantee skill was also long enough to keep the number of new masters low. Nor did guilds always act as guardians of quality. In towns where masters sat on the council, guilds secured bans on the sale of goods from neighbouring villages, a measure that protected members' markets but had little to do with the quality of anything. The more productive question, then, is not whether guilds were cartels or guarantors but under what conditions one function came to dominate the other. Cities in which guilds had to bargain with strong rulers, for example, seem to have been more likely to keep their privileges tied to inspection and standards, while those in which guilds controlled the municipal government were more likely to use their power to exclude rivals.

stimuli.title: Do Mice Mislead?
stimuli.body:
Mice are cheap, quick to breed, and easy to study, which is why they became the standard first test of new drugs. Yet roughly nine of every ten drug candidates that show promise in laboratory mice fail when they are tested in humans. Some researchers conclude that the mouse is simply the wrong tool: its biology differs from ours in ways that matter, and decades of effort have been wasted on a model that cannot predict human responses. A frequently cited example concerns sepsis, a life-threatening reaction to infection. When scientists compared gene-activity patterns in mice with those of human patients, they found almost no resemblance, and dozens of treatments that had rescued mice did nothing for people.

Defenders of animal research reply that the real problem lies not in the species but in the way the experiments are run. Surveys of published mouse studies show that many used very small groups, did not assign animals to treatment at random, and did not keep the experimenters ignorant of which animals had received the drug. Such practices are known to inflate apparent benefits, because an unconscious preference for the hoped-for result can shape how animals are selected and how outcomes are scored. In one analysis, studies that adopted randomization and blinding reported effects roughly half as large as those that did not. If most published successes in mice are exaggerated, the argument goes, it is hardly surprising that they fail to carry over to patients.

Both camps have a point, but neither fully explains the failures. Better design plainly matters, yet the sepsis case cannot be rescued by it: the mismatch there was detected in careful comparisons, and it concerned the very biological pathways the drugs were meant to target. Conversely, the pessimists overlook the fact that mouse results have proved more dependable for some questions, such as whether a compound reaches a particular organ, than for others, such as how the immune system responds to infection. A sensible conclusion is that the mouse should be trusted for what it has been shown to predict, with rigorous design as a precondition, and should not be treated as a stand-in for the human body in general.

stimuli.title: The Case for a Little Slack
stimuli.body:
Since the 1980s, the management literature has been dominated by the case against slack. Surplus staff, idle machines, and unspent budgets are, on this view, simply waste, and an organization that removes them becomes both cheaper and more disciplined. Few executives would defend the opposite position, at least in public. Lean production methods, borrowed from manufacturing, made the view seem almost self-evident, and consultants routinely treat a company's health as a matter of how little it keeps in reserve.

A minority of organizational theorists nevertheless argue that slack does useful work. Spare resources let a firm absorb a sudden shock, such as the failure of a supplier, without cutting staff, and they allow managers to fund experiments whose payoff is uncertain and which would never survive a strict budget review. Slack, in this reading, is the price of adaptability rather than a sign of indiscipline. Defenders of this view point to studies finding that firms with a moderate cushion of uncommitted resources introduce more new products than leaner rivals. Critics counter that such studies often measure slack by a firm's financial ratios, which may reflect past success rather than any decision to keep resources in reserve. A profitable firm will naturally have spare cash, and it would also have the means to innovate whether or not the cash sits idle.

What both camps tend to overlook is that slack is not one thing. Some slack is already absorbed into the firm's routines, such as redundant employees or generous overhead, and it is hard to redeploy; other slack, such as cash or unused credit, is uncommitted and can be put to any use. The first kind may indeed breed complacency, because people who are comfortable have little reason to change. The second kind is more likely to support experimentation, because it can be directed to new projects without anyone's job being threatened. Evidence from firms that cut headcount in a downturn is consistent with this distinction: those that preserved cash reserves while trimming staff recovered more quickly than those that did the opposite. Cushions of one kind can help while cushions of another kind hurt, and a debate that lumps them together will keep producing contradictory findings. If so, the real managerial question is not how much slack to hold but in what form to hold it.

stimuli.title: Fidelity and Its Discontents
stimuli.body:
A familiar complaint about translated literature holds that something is always lost. The poet's rhythm, the pun that depends on a double meaning, the words whose connotations belong to one culture alone: none of these can cross a language boundary intact. On this view the ideal translation is a transparent window onto the original, and every departure from it, however elegant, is a small betrayal. Readers who know both languages often feel this most acutely, and some refuse to read translations at all.

A newer school of translation scholars rejects the window metaphor. Translators, they point out, constantly make choices that the original does not dictate. A translator who renders a sixteenth-century poem in plain modern idiom is not failing to be faithful but deciding what fidelity should mean. These scholars propose that a translation is best seen as a new work, an idea drawn from a long tradition of regarding translators as authors in their own right rather than as clerks, written in the target language for readers with different expectations and judged by whether it lives as literature there. Support comes from the history of famous translations, several of which have been admired in their own right even by scholars who acknowledge that they depart widely from their sources.

The newer view corrects a real error, but it purchases its advantages at a cost its proponents rarely acknowledge. If a translation is simply a new work, there is no longer any clear sense in which one translation can be a better rendering of a given text than another; a version that bears no resemblance to the source would be as good a translation as a close one, provided it reads well. Yet readers who pick up a translation usually do so in order to encounter the author who wrote the original, and they would feel cheated to learn that the translator had invented freely. It seems better to say that translators serve two masters, the source and the target readers, whose demands cannot always be reconciled, and that the best translations are those that make the compromise visible and defensible rather than pretending it away. Neither pure fidelity nor pure freedom, in other words, is a coherent ideal on its own.

stimuli.title: What a Survival Rate Hides
stimuli.body:
Advocates of cancer screening often cite five-year survival rates. If a screening programme detects tumours earlier, patients diagnosed through it will, on average, be alive five years after diagnosis more often than patients whose cancers came to light only when symptoms appeared. The figure looks like clear evidence that screening saves lives, and it has the added appeal of being easy to calculate from routine hospital records, without any need to follow patients who were never diagnosed.

Statisticians point out two ways in which this evidence misleads. The first is lead-time bias. Suppose a tumour will cause death in the same year whether or not it is detected. Screening can find it years before symptoms would have, and the patient's survival "from diagnosis" is lengthened even though the date of death is unchanged; the clock simply started sooner. The second is overdiagnosis. Screening also finds abnormalities that are technically cancers but grow so slowly, or so rarely progress, that they would never have caused harm in the patient's lifetime. Every such person is counted as a survivor, which inflates the survival rate, yet each may be exposed to surgery or radiation with real side effects.

For this reason many epidemiologists prefer to compare death rates from the disease in screened and unscreened populations. Because this measure ignores when a diagnosis occurred, it is immune to both distortions. It has drawbacks of its own, however. Deaths from any given cancer are relatively rare, so a trial must follow a very large number of people for many years to detect a difference, and by the time results are published, treatments may have improved enough that the findings no longer describe current practice. Nor is a lower disease-specific death rate conclusive by itself: if complications from follow-up treatment cause deaths that are recorded under other headings, a programme could appear to succeed while doing little net good.

None of this shows that screening is worthless, and some programmes have reduced mortality convincingly. It shows only that a headline survival figure cannot, on its own, tell patients or policymakers whether a given programme is worth its costs.

stimuli.title: The Bilingual Advantage Revisited
stimuli.body:
Early studies of bilingual children reported a striking benefit: constant switching between two languages seemed to train the executive functions, such as ignoring distractions and shifting attention, that underlie planning and self-control. The finding spread quickly beyond the laboratory into parenting guides and school policy. More recent work has been less kind. Several large studies found no difference between bilingual and monolingual children, and a review of published research noted that studies reporting a bilingual advantage were far more likely to appear in journals than studies reporting none, suggesting that the early literature may have been skewed by what got published.

Defenders of the advantage reply that the later null results do not necessarily contradict the earlier ones. Tasks that measure executive function vary widely, and the benefit may appear only in tasks that demand heavy conflict monitoring and only among children who switch languages often, a condition that many large samples do not control. Sceptics answer that a hypothesis narrowed in this way after the fact risks becoming unfalsifiable: whenever a study finds no effect, one can say that the wrong task or the wrong children were measured. A fair verdict is that the advantage, if it exists, is more limited than first claimed, and that settling the question will require studies that specify in advance which children and which tasks should show the effect.

stimuli.title: Pricing One Side of a Platform
stimuli.body:
A conventional test for predatory pricing asks whether a firm is selling a product below its cost, on the theory that only a firm hoping to drive out rivals and later raise prices would accept such losses. Applied to a firm that sells a single product to a single group of customers, the test is sensible.

It is far less reliable when applied to platforms that serve two groups at once, such as an online marketplace that connects buyers with sellers. Each group values the platform more when the other group is larger, so the platform must attract both. Typically one side is more sensitive to price, or more valuable to the other side, and the platform charges that side little or nothing, recovering its costs from the other. A marketplace that lets shoppers browse free while charging sellers a commission is "selling below cost" to shoppers by the conventional test, yet it is the shoppers' presence that makes the platform worth paying for.

Some competition authorities have responded by assessing a platform's revenues and costs as a whole. This is more defensible, but it has difficulties of its own. Shared costs, such as the servers and engineers that serve both groups, can be allocated between the two sides only in a largely arbitrary way, and a platform that really is pursuing a predatory strategy can disguise it by describing the losses on one side as an investment in network effects. A further complication is that a pricing structure that is benign in a mature platform may be harmful in a new market, where subsidised users can be locked in before a rival has had the chance to reach the scale it needs.

The upshot is not that platform pricing should be exempt from scrutiny. It is that the useful question is whether the pricing would make sense for a platform with no plan to eliminate competitors, and that this is an empirical matter on which a bright-line rule is of little use. Regulators who want a simple number to apply will be disappointed, but the alternative of applying the simple test to a complicated business is worse.

stimuli.title: How Safe Is Safe Enough?
stimuli.body:
Developers of self-driving vehicles often argue that their systems should be judged against human drivers, and that if the machine is safer, even if not perfect, then deploying it is justified. The logic is appealing, but it is far harder to apply than it sounds. A fleet that has driven a million miles without a serious crash, for instance, tells us surprisingly little about whether it is safer than people.

Consider first the problem of measurement. Fatal crashes among human drivers are rare, on the order of one for every hundred million miles. To show with confidence that an automated system is at least as safe, it would have to be driven hundreds of millions of miles, which at the pace of a test fleet would take many years. The arithmetic is unforgiving: a record of zero deaths over a few million miles is compatible with a system far worse than the human average. Companies therefore rely on indirect evidence, such as the frequency of minor incidents or of occasions on which the human safety driver takes over, but such measures do not translate reliably into fatalities.

Second, there is the problem of comparison. The human average includes drunk, drowsy, and distracted drivers, as well as drivers on the most dangerous roads in the worst weather. Test miles by automated systems have mostly been driven in good weather, on carefully mapped roads, and with a safety driver ready to intervene. A system that is safer than the average human under these conditions may not be safer than an attentive, sober human anywhere. Some analysts therefore argue that automated vehicles should have to match a careful driver, not the average one.

A stricter standard has its own cost, however. If an automated system were safer than the average driver but not as safe as the best, holding it back would leave the average driver on the road, with all the deaths that implies. The more reasonable conclusion is that no single benchmark can settle the matter in advance. Staged deployment, in which vehicles are introduced in limited settings and monitored continuously, would generate the evidence that testing alone cannot, while limiting the harm if early assumptions prove wrong.

stimuli.title: Cleaning the Old Masters
stimuli.body:
When conservators remove the yellowed varnish from an old painting, the colours beneath often appear startlingly bright, and the public reaction is frequently one of alarm. Critics charge that cleaning strips away not only dirt and discoloured varnish but also thin translucent layers of paint, called glazes, with which the artist modelled shadows, and that what is revealed is a harsh surface the painter never intended. Some go further, claiming that viewers have grown accustomed to the warm brown tone of aged pictures and that this tone has become part of each work's identity.

Conservators answer that the varnish is not part of the original object: it was applied to protect the paint and was always expected to be replaced once it darkened. Modern solvent tests and microscopic examination of paint cross-sections, they say, allow them to stop at the original paint with far greater precision than earlier generations managed.

The dispute is partly about facts and partly about values. Whether a particular cleaning has removed original glaze is a matter that analysis of paint samples can in principle decide. Whether a viewer ought to prefer the picture as the artist painted it to the picture as centuries have shaped it, however, cannot be settled by any test, and the claim that the aged tone has acquired a legitimacy of its own deserves more respect than conservators sometimes allow.

stimuli.title: Does Language Shape What We See?
stimuli.body:
The idea that the language one speaks shapes how one perceives the world has a long and troubled history. In its strong form, which holds that language determines thought and that speakers of different languages inhabit incommensurable mental worlds, it has few defenders today. Its main weakness is empirical: people can plainly think about distinctions their own language does not mark, as shown by the ease with which they learn words for them.

A weaker version has fared better. Experiments on colour perception are the best-known evidence. Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, whereas English uses a single word for both. Russian speakers, researchers found, are quicker to tell two shades of blue apart when the shades fall on opposite sides of that lexical boundary, while English speakers show no comparable advantage. The effect vanishes, however, when participants are asked to repeat a string of digits while they work, a task that occupies the verbal system. This suggests that language does not alter the visual experience itself but supplies a quick label that is used in judgements whenever it is available.

Sceptics raise two objections. First, effects of this sort are small, measured in fractions of a second, and have proved difficult to replicate in some laboratories. Second, the results are open to a different interpretation: cultures that distinguish more shades may do so because their members have more reason to discuss them, in which case the vocabulary reflects experience rather than creating the difference. The first objection deserves to be taken seriously. The second is less damaging than it seems, because the digit-repetition result is hard to explain if the difference lay in the speakers' perceptual experience alone; that experience is not changed by occupying the verbal system for a few moments.

The most defensible conclusion is therefore a modest one. Language may not determine what people see, but it appears to provide a tool for quick comparison that people use when circumstances allow. Whether even that modest claim survives will depend on larger replications, preferably across many languages and many colour boundaries of different kinds.

stimuli.title: One Number for Loyalty
stimuli.body:
Many companies track customer loyalty with a single question: how likely is the customer to recommend the firm to a friend or colleague? The answers are boiled down to one score, and its popularity owes much to a claim that it predicts a firm's growth better than longer satisfaction surveys do. Subsequent academic tests have mostly failed to confirm that claim. Across industries, the single score predicted revenue growth no better than conventional measures, and in several industries it predicted growth worse.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that the measure is useless. Its defenders argue that its real contribution lies not in forecasting accuracy but in organizational behaviour. A single number is easy for frontline staff to understand, simple to track daily, and hard to bury in a sixty-page report; firms that adopt it often find that managers who ignored the findings of earlier surveys begin to act on them. If so, the measure may improve outcomes not because it captures something that other surveys miss but because it is actually used. This is a plausible suggestion, though one that has not been tested directly. Testing it would require comparing firms that adopt the simple score with otherwise similar firms that adopt an equally simple but less predictive measure, and few studies have done so.

stimuli.title: The Vitamin D Puzzle
stimuli.body:
For two decades, studies that followed large groups of people reported that those with higher blood levels of vitamin D had lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, and several cancers. The finding led many physicians to recommend supplements widely, since the vitamin is cheap and the recommendation seemed to carry little downside. More recently, large randomized trials, in which participants were assigned by lot to take either vitamin D or a placebo, have mostly found that supplements do not prevent these diseases.

The discrepancy has a well-known explanation. Observational studies cannot separate vitamin D from the habits that accompany it. People with high levels tend to spend more time outdoors, exercise more, and weigh less. Chronic illness can itself lower vitamin D, since sick people spend less time in the sun. In such cases the vitamin is a marker of health rather than a cause of it. Healthier people differ from less healthy people in many ways besides their vitamin D, and no statistical adjustment can capture all of them. Randomization removes these confounding factors, which is why the trial results are generally given more weight.

Yet it would be hasty to conclude that vitamin D is irrelevant to health. Most trial participants were not deficient to begin with; many were healthy volunteers, and a number were already taking supplements on their own. A trial in which nearly everyone has an adequate level at the outset can show, at most, that adding more vitamin D to an adequate supply does little. In effect, the trials tested a narrower question than the one the observational studies seemed to raise. They cannot show that correcting a true deficiency is pointless, and few trials have been large enough to study deficient people on their own. Such trials are also hard to run, because many researchers consider it unethical to give a placebo to someone known to be deficient.

The honest summary, then, for patients and physicians who must decide today, is that routine supplementation for the general public is not supported by the evidence, while the case for treating people with demonstrated deficiency remains open.

stimuli.title: The Price of a Rainy Evening
stimuli.body:
When demand for a service spikes, as it does for ride-hailing on a rainy evening, many platforms raise prices automatically. Ride-hailing firms were among the first to make the practice routine, though airlines and hotels have long used versions of it. Economists tend to approve. Higher prices ration limited supply to those who value it most and, equally important, call forth additional supply, since drivers are drawn onto the road by the prospect of higher earnings. A fixed price, by contrast, leaves the market short of drivers exactly when they are most needed, and the shortage is resolved through long waits that fall on everyone.

Customers, however, often react with anger, and surveys consistently show that many regard surge pricing as exploitative, with resentment strongest when a surge coincides with bad weather or a public emergency and customers feel they have little choice. Some economists dismiss this reaction as a failure to understand markets. That dismissal is too quick. Research on consumer fairness norms suggests that people accept price increases that track a firm's costs but resent increases that merely exploit their lack of alternatives. A rainy evening raises the customer's urgency, not the cost to the firm of providing the ride, and so the increase is seen as opportunism. The reaction matters commercially, too: customers who feel exploited may switch to a competitor with a more predictable fare structure, even if that competitor is slower to respond to changes in demand.

None of this means that firms should abandon dynamic pricing. It suggests that the way prices change matters as much as whether they change. Firms have experimented with caps on multipliers, with showing the price before the ride is confirmed, and with presenting off-peak fares as discounts rather than peak fares as surcharges, a reframing that leaves the economics unchanged yet appears to reduce resentment. Whether such measures are enough remains an open question, because most of the evidence on them comes from short experiments, and trust is built or lost over years. Firms that treat fairness as a constraint to be managed, not an irrationality to be ignored, are likely to do better.

stimuli.title: Why Do Foragers Share?
stimuli.body:
Among many foraging peoples, a successful hunter does not keep the meat of a large animal; it is distributed to the whole camp, often by rules that give the hunter himself no special portion. Anthropologists have offered several explanations. The oldest holds that sharing is a form of insurance. Large game is caught rarely and unpredictably, so a hunter who is lucky today may be unlucky next month, and by giving away meat he secures a claim on the catch of others when his own luck fails. On this reciprocity account, sharing is self-interested, and each person's generosity is repaid.

A second explanation, tolerated theft, notes that the meat of a large animal cannot be stored and that a hunter who tried to guard it would spend more effort defending it than it was worth. Sharing is then not generosity but the best of a bad set of options, a concession to the demands of onlookers. Observers who have watched foragers closely sometimes report exactly such pressure: hunters slow to hand over meat are teased, and those who are persistently stingy are shunned.

A third account stresses signalling. Hunters, on this view, share lavishly because success in hunting, and the willingness to give the proceeds away, advertises qualities that others value in allies and mates. Evidence for this theory is mixed. Good hunters do appear to enjoy extra status and more partners, but the theory struggles to explain why the meat is frequently distributed by someone other than the hunter, a practice that would seem to deprive him of credit.

Each account captures something real, yet none explains the pattern of sharing alone. Reciprocity predicts that sharing should be proportional to what one has given, but studies often find that sharing is only weakly related to past contributions. Tolerated theft predicts that sharing should be strongest for resources that cannot be hidden or stored, but the sharing of easily concealed items such as honey has often been reported to follow similar rules. A satisfactory account probably has to combine the insurance logic with norms enforced by the group, so that sharing is sustained not by any single motive but by a system of expectations that is costly to violate.

stimuli.title: Tears for Anna Karenina
stimuli.body:
Readers weep over the deaths of characters they know to be invented, and philosophers have long found this puzzling. If we believe that Anna Karenina does not exist, how can we pity her? The usual assumption is that genuine pity requires a belief in the sufferer's reality. One response denies that readers' emotions are genuine: what they feel is a pretend or quasi-emotion, a make-believe counterpart that lacks the motivation to act that real pity has. This would explain why no one calls the police when a character is murdered.

The response has a cost, however. Readers' tears are real tears, and their hearts do race; the reaction is physiologically indistinguishable from the response to a real tragedy. A rival view holds instead that the belief requirement is false. Emotions, it says, can be prompted by vividly imagined situations, just as a person may be frightened by a vivid memory of a danger that is no longer present. On this account the emotions are genuine but are directed at imagined scenarios, and they do not lead to action because we recognize that nothing can be done for a character on a page.

The rival view has its own difficulty: it seems to make our engagement with fiction continuous with daydreaming, yet few readers would say that a daydream moves them as a novel does. Perhaps the best that can be said is that fiction offers a structured, shared imagining, in which an author's craft guides our attention toward suffering in a way that our private fantasies seldom manage.

stimuli.title: Are Electric Cars Really Cleaner?
stimuli.body:
Electric vehicles are often described as zero-emission, a phrase that refers only to what comes out of the tailpipe. The label is nevertheless repeated in advertising and, more importantly, in the rules for some purchase subsidies. Sceptics respond that the claim ignores two sources of emissions elsewhere: the energy-intensive manufacture of the battery, which means an electric car leaves the factory carrying a larger carbon burden than a petrol car, and the generation of the electricity used to charge it, which in some regions comes mainly from burning coal.

Life-cycle analyses, which add up emissions from manufacture through driving to disposal, have generally found that electric cars still come out ahead. The battery's extra burden is repaid by lower emissions per kilometre, usually within a few years of typical driving, and the advantage then widens with every additional kilometre; the margin depends on the petrol vehicle being replaced, since a small hatchback and a large sport-utility vehicle differ greatly. Critics reply that such studies tend to assume average driving distances and average electricity grids; an electric car that is driven little, charged on a coal-heavy grid, and fitted with a very large battery may never recoup its head start.

Both sides are, in a sense, right, and the dispute is better understood as a disagreement about which cases to treat as typical. The break-even point can be calculated for any combination of grid, battery size, and mileage, and it varies enormously: under favourable conditions it arrives within two years, while under unfavourable ones it may not arrive within the car's lifetime. What neither side emphasises enough is that the grid is not fixed. An electric car bought today will be charged for a decade or more, during which the grid in most countries is expected to draw on a growing share of lower-emission generation, whereas a petrol car's emissions per kilometre will stay roughly constant. This shifts the balance toward electric cars in many places. But it depends on a forecast that cannot be certain, and it does not rescue the case for very large batteries in vehicles that are used only lightly.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that cities should replace white LED lamps with a different kind of lighting
demonstrate that moths are more effective pollinators than bees and hoverflies
describe a study that challenges a casual assumption about artificial light and moths, and note objections to how its results should be read
explain why moths are attracted to artificial light in the first place
show that seed production is an unreliable measure of the health of plant populations
questions.explanation:
The first paragraph overturns the assumption that light-driven moth loss is minor, using the meadow study. The second gives the authors' interpretation and the third gives the critics' objections plus the authors' reply. Choice C captures that whole arc.

A is a policy recommendation the passage never makes; the LED detail is incidental. B is not claimed; the passage says daytime insects cannot replace moths for some plants, not that moths are better overall. D treats the attraction of moths to light as the topic, but the passage takes that as already known. E reflects one critic's minor point, not the passage as a whole.
questions.tip: Summarise the passage's three-step arc (claim, evidence, objection) before looking at purpose choices.
questions.trap: Choice about seed production being unreliable: it picks up one critic's point and inflates it into the passage's purpose.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the authors respond to the objection that moths may merely have moved between plots by pointing out that
choices: moth visits to the dark plots were higher than visits to the lit plots
the lit plots and the dark plots were separated by a considerable distance
bees and hoverflies visited the lit plots as often as they visited the dark plots
seedlings in the lit plots faced less competition than seedlings in the dark plots
seed output in the dark plots did not rise above the regional norm
questions.explanation:
The last paragraph says the authors "note that seed output in the dark plots did not rise above the regional norm, as a simple redistribution would predict." That is E.

A is true (moth visits fell in the lit plots, so they were higher in the dark ones), but that is the result the critics call ambiguous, not the authors' reply to the objection. B contradicts the passage, which says the plots were close together. C is true (daytime visits were the same) but belongs to the study results, not the reply to this objection. D is the critics' second point, about seedling competition, not the authors' reply.
questions.tip: For detail questions tied to a named response, find the sentence beginning with the authors' rebuttal and match it almost word for word.
questions.trap: Choosing what the objection would predict instead of what the authors actually reported.

questions.prompt: The author mentions the daytime visits by bees and hoverflies most likely in order to
choices: rule out a general fall in insect activity as the explanation for reduced seed output in the lit plots
suggest that bees and hoverflies are less important pollinators than moths for most plants
support the critics' claim that visits were simply redistributed between plots
show that white LED lamps attract daytime insects as strongly as they attract moths
indicate that daytime pollinators made up for the lost night visits in the lit plots
questions.explanation:
Daytime visits were "the same in both kinds of plot," so the lamps did not disturb insects generally, and daytime insects did not make up for the missing night visits. The seed shortfall therefore points to the loss of moths, which is A.

B goes beyond the passage; it says nothing about "most plants". C has no link to the unchanged daytime figures. D is wrong because equal daytime visits show the lamps did not affect daytime insects at all, so they cannot show that the lamps attract them. E is the opposite: seeds fell, so no compensation occurred.
questions.tip: When a detail is introduced with "even though", ask what alternative explanation it eliminates.
questions.trap: Choosing the compensation answer, which confuses unchanged daytime visits with extra daytime visits.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that acquiring firms are less competent than other firms
demonstrate that auctions are an unreliable way of selling companies
show that target shareholders benefit more from takeovers than acquirer shareholders do
assess two explanations for the poor returns earned by acquiring firms and suggest that both may contribute
refute the winner's curse explanation of takeover outcomes
questions.explanation:
The passage introduces the winner's curse, shows where it falls short, offers the hubris hypothesis, and concludes both may operate. That is D.

A contradicts the first paragraph, which says acquirers are "no less competent" on the winner's-curse account. B is not the passage's concern; auctions are only the setting for one hypothesis. C is a starting observation, not what the passage sets out to do. E is too strong; the author says the curse "cannot be the entire story", not that it is wrong.
questions.tip: On "evaluate competing explanations" passages, the author usually lands on a qualified middle position; be suspicious of choices with "refute" or "demonstrate".
questions.trap: "Refute" sounds decisive, but the author keeps the winner's curse in the final sentence.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the winner's curse explanation would most likely predict that, other things being equal, returns to an acquirer would be
choices: lower when the target negotiates with a single bidder than when it faces several
less negative when the target negotiates with a single bidder than when it faces several
unaffected by the number of firms competing for the target
higher when the bidding firm has more capable executives
higher when the target's true value is harder to estimate
questions.explanation:
The author says that if the curse were the whole story, overpayment "should largely disappear" with a lone bidder. So returns should be less negative in uncontested deals: B.

A reverses the prediction. C contradicts it entirely, since the curse depends on selection from several bidders. D brings in executive ability, which the winner's-curse account explicitly sets aside ("no less competent"). E has it backwards; greater uncertainty widens the spread of estimates and worsens the curse.
questions.tip: For "predict" questions, restate the author's own "if X were true, we would see Y" sentence in plain words first.
questions.trap: The reversed answer is tempting if you misread "disappear" as applying to contested auctions.

questions.prompt: The author states that hubris "is usually inferred from the very outcomes it is meant to explain" in order to
choices: suggest that executives are unaware of their own overconfidence
argue that returns in uncontested deals are not reliable evidence
support the claim that the winner's curse is the more important cause
point to a difficulty in testing the hubris hypothesis independently
show that the hubris hypothesis can be ruled out as an explanation
questions.explanation:
The clause appears right after "harder to test." If hubris is measured by the poor outcomes it is supposed to cause, the reasoning is circular, so independent testing is difficult. That is D.

A is not discussed; the passage is about measurement, not executives' self-awareness. B confuses the target of the remark; the data are not criticised. C runs the other way; the author thinks hubris explains uncontested deals better. E is far too strong; the author keeps hubris in the final view.
questions.tip: A quoted phrase in a function question is usually the author's reason for a stated limitation; read the sentence just before it.
questions.trap: Choosing "ruled out" mistakes a testing difficulty for a refutation.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: defend the view that medieval guilds were mainly guarantors of product quality
argue that a debate about the role of guilds has been framed too narrowly and propose a more useful question
show that Adam Smith's criticism of trade associations was well founded
describe how the apprenticeship system of medieval guilds worked
demonstrate that guilds in cities with strong rulers never excluded competitors
questions.explanation:
Paragraphs one and two set out the cartel and guarantor views; paragraph three says both are incomplete, "a mistake to treat them as exclusive alternatives," and proposes asking when one function dominated. That is B.

A is the revisionist side, which the author qualifies rather than defends. C gets the author's stance wrong; Smith is cited as an echo of the older view, not endorsed. D is one detail serving the revisionist argument, not the point of the passage. E is far too strong; the author says such cities were "more likely" to keep standards, not that they never excluded rivals.
questions.tip: When a passage ends with "the more productive question is...", the purpose is usually to reframe a debate.
questions.trap: Choosing one side of the two-sided debate, when the author deliberately stands above it.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the economic historians who offer the more recent reading cite which of the following as evidence for their view?
choices: Guilds forbade members to adopt new production techniques
Guilds obtained bans on the sale of goods from neighbouring villages
Masters frequently sat on town councils
Guild-stamped goods often sold for higher prices in distant markets
Apprenticeships were generally short enough to admit many new masters
questions.explanation:
Paragraph two ends with the supporting evidence: guild-stamped goods "often fetched higher prices in distant markets." That is D.

A belongs to the older cartel view in paragraph one. B and C come from the author's own paragraph three, where they show guilds acting against competitors. E contradicts paragraph three, which says apprenticeships were long enough to keep entry low.
questions.tip: In detail questions that name a group, make sure the evidence comes from that group's paragraph, not from the author's own commentary.
questions.trap: Choosing a fact that appears in the passage but is attributed to the other side.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree with which of the following?
choices: Guilds located in cities with strong rulers never fixed prices
Adam Smith's complaint about trade associations had no basis in medieval practice
Guild-stamped goods were of higher quality than non-guild goods in every town
Bans on goods from neighbouring villages were mainly intended to raise quality
A single guild rule could both assure buyers of quality and limit competition among sellers
questions.explanation:
The author says the long apprenticeship that guaranteed skill "was also long enough to keep the number of new masters low." One rule, two effects: E.

A overstates; the passage says only that such guilds "seem to have been more likely" to stay tied to standards. B is contradicted by the third paragraph, where guilds do protect members' markets. C is not supported; the passage gives no comparison for every town. D reverses the passage, which says the bans had "little to do with the quality of anything".
questions.tip: The safest inference is often a modest restatement of two facts the author has already placed side by side.
questions.trap: Absolute words such as "never" and "every" signal that an inference choice outruns the passage.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if discovered about a particular medieval town, would most support the author's suggestion about the conditions under which guilds acted chiefly as cartels?
choices: Master craftsmen dominated the town council, and the guilds repeatedly obtained bans on the sale of competing goods from nearby villages
Guilds in the town bargained with a strong ruler and, as a condition of their privileges, agreed to inspect all goods before sale
Goods bearing the town's guild stamp fetched higher prices in distant markets than unstamped goods
The town's guilds expelled members found cheating, and the fines collected were used to pay for inspectors
The town's guilds shortened apprenticeships after a plague reduced the number of skilled workers
questions.explanation:
The author suggests guilds were more likely to exclude rivals where they "controlled the municipal government." Council domination plus bans on rival goods fits that exactly: A.

B, C and D each illustrate the guarantor function (inspection, price premiums, discipline of cheats), which the author ties to guilds that had to bargain with strong rulers. E concerns entry, but says nothing about who controlled the government, so it does not show cartel behaviour.
questions.tip: In application questions, map the options onto the author's two conditions (strong ruler / guild-run government) and pick the one that matches the condition asked about.
questions.trap: Choosing a guarantor-side fact because it sounds like medieval guild evidence, when the question asks about cartels.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that animal research should be abandoned in favour of studies on human patients
explain why small sample sizes cause most drug trials to fail
present two explanations for why drugs that work in mice often fail in humans and argue that neither is sufficient on its own
report a new analysis showing that randomization and blinding halve the benefits of drugs
describe the biological differences between the immune systems of mice and humans
questions.explanation:
Paragraph one gives the pessimists' explanation (wrong species), paragraph two gives the defenders' explanation (poor design), and paragraph three says "neither fully explains the failures." That is C.

A goes further than the author, who recommends trusting the mouse for what it predicts. B narrows to one factor and to mouse studies, not drug trials in general. D turns a supporting statistic into the main point; it also is not the author's own analysis. E is a detail about sepsis and immune responses, not the overall aim.
questions.tip: When the final paragraph begins "Both camps have a point", the purpose is evaluative: present two views, then qualify both.
questions.trap: Choosing the statistic about randomization, which is vivid but only supports one side.

questions.prompt: The author discusses the sepsis case in the third paragraph primarily in order to
choices: provide further evidence that mouse studies are generally unreliable
show that improving experimental design cannot fully account for the failure of mouse results to carry over to humans
illustrate a condition for which mice have proved dependable guides
argue that gene-activity comparisons are the best way of validating a model
suggest that sepsis treatments should be tested first on human patients
questions.explanation:
The third paragraph says "Better design plainly matters, yet the sepsis case cannot be rescued by it," because the mismatch showed up in careful comparisons. So sepsis is used as a limit on the defenders' argument: B.

A is what the pessimists claim; the author rejects such sweeping distrust. C reverses the case; sepsis is where mice predicted poorly. D is not suggested. E also falls outside the passage, which makes no recommendation about the order of testing.
questions.tip: Ask which side of the debate an example is being used against; the sentence that introduces it usually says.
questions.trap: Treating the sepsis example as supporting the pessimists, when the author uses it only to limit the defenders.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that mouse studies conducted without randomization and blinding are likely to
choices: have used larger groups of animals than other studies
identify mismatches in biological pathways more often
be less likely to reach publication
overstate the benefit of the treatment being tested
produce results that are reliable for predicting how a compound reaches an organ
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph says these practices "inflate apparent benefits" and that studies using them reported effects "roughly half as large" when they were not used. So such studies likely overstate benefits: D.

A contradicts the passage, which links the lack of randomization to very small groups. B is unsupported; pathway mismatch was found in careful comparisons. C publication is never discussed (the surveys concern published studies). E mixes up the point; the passage says organ-reach predictions are dependable for mice generally, not for poorly designed studies.
questions.tip: For "suggests" questions, find the sentence that states cause and effect and restate it in the question's terms.
questions.trap: The organ-reach choice borrows a favourable phrase from paragraph three and attaches it to the wrong group.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument made by the defenders of animal research in the second paragraph?
choices: Drug candidates tested in well-designed, randomized and blinded mouse experiments failed in human trials at about the same rate as candidates tested in poorly designed experiments
Most drug candidates that later failed in human trials had been tested in mouse studies that were neither randomized nor blinded
Mouse studies that used larger groups of animals reported smaller benefits than studies that used small groups
Experimenters who knew which animals had received a drug tended to score outcomes more favourably
Some researchers who ran poorly designed mouse studies were unaware that blinding was recommended
questions.explanation:
The defenders argue that exaggerated results from weak design explain failures in humans. If well-designed studies fail at the same rate as weak ones, design cannot be the explanation, so A weakens the argument most.

B strengthens it by tying failures to weak design. C and D also strengthen it by showing that weak practices inflate results. E is irrelevant to whether design explains the failures; it concerns researchers' awareness.
questions.tip: To weaken a "design explains failure" claim, show failure persists when design is good.
questions.trap: Options that merely repeat the flaws of poor design strengthen the argument, even though they sound critical.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: recommend that firms hold as much spare cash as possible in order to fund innovation
summarize several decades of research on lean management and its effects on profitability
show that profitable firms are better at innovation than unprofitable firms
explain why executives are reluctant to defend slack in public
argue that a prevailing view of organizational slack overlooks a distinction that may help reconcile conflicting evidence
questions.explanation:
Paragraph one gives the standard case against slack, paragraph two the opposing studies and the critics' reply, and paragraph three introduces the absorbed/uncommitted distinction as something "both camps tend to overlook." That is E.

A goes beyond the passage; the author says form matters more than amount, not that more is better. B is too broad, since the passage covers only the slack debate. C is the critics' suspicion, not the author's thesis. D is a passing remark in paragraph one, not the focus.
questions.tip: When the author says "both camps overlook," the purpose is to introduce a distinction that reframes the debate.
questions.trap: The "hold as much cash as possible" choice turns a distinction into an extreme recommendation.

questions.prompt: The author mentions firms that cut headcount in a downturn most likely in order to
choices: demonstrate that complacency is the main cause of failure in lean organizations
show that the critics' objection about financial ratios is mistaken
offer evidence that fits the proposed distinction between kinds of slack
argue that firms should avoid cutting staff under all circumstances
illustrate how a supplier failure can be absorbed without layoffs
questions.explanation:
The author introduces this evidence as "consistent with this distinction": firms that kept cash while trimming staff recovered faster. The point is to support the absorbed versus uncommitted split, as in C.

A overstates; complacency is only said to be a possible effect of absorbed slack. B is not addressed by this evidence; the author never calls the critics mistaken. D contradicts the example, in which staff were trimmed and recovery was better. E is from paragraph two and concerns a different example.
questions.tip: The words "consistent with" tell you an example is supporting evidence for the point just made.
questions.trap: The choice about supplier failures lifts a detail from the right topic but the wrong paragraph.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that the critics mentioned in the second paragraph would be most likely to agree with which of the following?
choices: Firms with moderate slack do not introduce more new products than leaner rivals
Financial ratios can show that a firm has spare resources without showing that the firm chose to keep them in reserve
Profitable firms innovate less than unprofitable firms because they have more cash
Managers should fund uncertain experiments only from uncommitted resources
Removing surplus staff and idle machines never lowers costs
questions.explanation:
The critics say financial ratios "may reflect past success rather than any decision to keep resources in reserve." That is exactly B.

A is too strong; the critics question what the studies show, not whether the pattern exists. C is reversed and not stated; they say profitable firms would innovate regardless. D is the author's distinction, not the critics' claim. E contradicts the first paragraph's mainstream view, which the critics are not said to reject.
questions.tip: Attribute inferences to the right speaker; "the critics" are not the author.
questions.trap: Choosing the author's own distinction (cash versus absorbed slack) and attributing it to the critics.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously undermine the author's claim in the last sentence that the form of slack matters more than its amount?
choices: Firms with redundant staff were slower to move people between projects than firms without redundant staff
Firms that cut headcount during the downturn reported greater employee anxiety in the following year
Moderate slack, as measured by financial ratios, was associated with more new products in the studies described
Across a large sample of firms, innovation rose with total slack and did not differ between firms holding mostly cash and firms holding mostly redundant staff
Many executives who publicly oppose slack privately keep small reserves of unspent budget
questions.explanation:
If innovation depends on the total amount of slack and not on whether it is cash or redundant staff, the form does not matter, which directly undermines the claim: D.

A is consistent with the author's point that absorbed slack is hard to redeploy. B concerns anxiety, not innovation or recovery. C is a result both the author and the defenders accept. E is about executives' private behaviour and says nothing about form versus amount.
questions.tip: To undermine "X matters more than Y", show that varying X while holding Y fixed changes nothing.
questions.trap: Evidence that moderate slack helps agrees with the defenders and with the author, so it cannot undermine the claim about form.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: defend the traditional view that every translation inevitably betrays its original
argue that famous translations should be judged by the same standards as original works
examine two ways of thinking about translation and argue for a modified view that accounts for what readers expect
show that translators of sixteenth-century poetry should use modern idiom
explain why puns and rhythms cannot be transferred from one language to another
questions.explanation:
Paragraph one gives the "window" view, paragraph two the "new work" view, and paragraph three criticises the second and proposes that translators "serve two masters." That is C.

A is the position the author modifies. B is the newer scholars' claim, which the author qualifies. D is only one example, offered by the newer scholars. E is a background point used to introduce the window view, not the passage's purpose.
questions.tip: In a passage with two schools and a third paragraph beginning "yet" or "but," the purpose is usually to evaluate and then synthesise.
questions.trap: Selecting the newer school's claim because it is the more detailed and appears to be the passage's centre of gravity.

questions.prompt: The author mentions a translator who renders a sixteenth-century poem in plain modern idiom primarily in order to
choices: criticize modern translators for ignoring the style of the original
provide an example of a translation that departs too far from its source
show that most famous translations were written in plain language
suggest that old poetry cannot be translated at all
illustrate the newer scholars' claim that fidelity is itself a matter of choice
questions.explanation:
The example follows the claim that translators make choices the original "does not dictate," and the sentence says the translator is "deciding what fidelity should mean." It illustrates the newer scholars' claim: E.

A is the opposite of what the sentence says; the translator is not described as failing. B is not the author's judgement here; the example appears in the newer scholars' paragraph. C is unsupported; famous translations are mentioned only as admired. D contradicts the passage, which discusses translating such poems.
questions.tip: Read the sentence before and after an example; the claim it illustrates is usually stated there.
questions.trap: Reading the example as a criticism, when the sentence describes the translator favourably.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author believes the newer view
choices: makes it hard to distinguish a close translation from a free invention in terms of quality as a translation
is mistaken in claiming that translators make choices the original does not dictate
undervalues the importance of literary merit in translated works
cannot be reconciled with the observation that some translations are admired in their own right
rests on the assumption that readers prefer plain modern idiom
questions.explanation:
The author says that on the newer view "a version that bears no resemblance to the source would be as good a translation as a close one." So the view blurs close translation and free invention: A.

B contradicts the author, who says the view "corrects a real error." C is the reverse of the author's complaint, since the view puts merit as literature first. D is not claimed; the author never denies that translations can be admired. E is not mentioned.
questions.tip: When an author says a view "corrects a real error but has a cost," the cost will be a logical consequence, found in the last paragraph.
questions.trap: Picking the answer about literary merit, which is exactly what the newer view values.

questions.prompt: The author's claim that, on the newer view, one translation can no longer be a better rendering than another depends on which of the following assumptions?
choices: Readers who pick up a translation cannot read the original language
The newer scholars' criteria for judging a translation do not include how closely it resembles the source
Every translation must choose between serving the source and serving the readers
Famous translations always depart widely from their sources
A translation that reads well in the target language must resemble its source
questions.explanation:
The author argues that a version bearing no resemblance to the source would count as good if it reads well. That works only if resemblance to the source is not among the newer scholars' criteria: B.

A is irrelevant to the argument about criteria. C is the author's own recommendation for the compromise, not a necessary assumption for the criticism. D is too strong ("always"), and the passage says only that several famous translations depart widely. E would remove the problem, since good reading would then guarantee resemblance.
questions.tip: An assumption question can be tested by negating the choice: if the argument collapses, you have the assumption.
questions.trap: The final answer choice would resolve the problem the author describes, so it cannot be the assumption.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: explain why a commonly cited statistic about screening can mislead and to discuss an alternative measure that has limitations of its own
argue that cancer screening programmes should be discontinued
show that lead-time bias is a more serious problem than overdiagnosis
report the results of a large trial comparing death rates in screened and unscreened groups
compare the five-year survival rates of fast-growing and slow-growing cancers
questions.explanation:
The passage presents survival rates, explains two distortions, offers death-rate comparisons, and notes that these also have drawbacks. That is A.

B is contradicted by the last paragraph ("None of this shows that screening is worthless"). C makes a ranking of the two biases that the author never offers. D is wrong because no trial is reported; the passage only discusses the measure. E is out of scope; no such comparison is made.
questions.tip: For a purpose question, notice the last paragraph's hedge ("None of this shows..."): it rules out any "argue to abolish" option.
questions.trap: Choosing the dramatic policy conclusion that the author explicitly disclaims.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, overdiagnosis inflates survival rates because
choices: screening shortens the interval between a diagnosis and a patient's death
people with abnormalities that would never have harmed them are counted among the survivors
patients treated after screening tend to be younger than those diagnosed by symptoms
follow-up treatments help patients live longer than they otherwise would
deaths from complications are recorded under other headings
questions.explanation:
The passage says that each person with a harmless, slow abnormality is "counted as a survivor, which inflates the survival rate." That is B.

A reverses lead-time bias; screening lengthens, not shortens, the interval from diagnosis. C is not mentioned. D is not claimed; the passage says such treatment has side effects. E concerns the death-rate measure in the third paragraph, not survival rates.
questions.tip: When a question asks "because", look for the causal word in the text and match it to the right distortion.
questions.trap: Mixing up lead-time bias with overdiagnosis, which the first answer does.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that "treatments may have improved" by the time trial results are published most likely in order to
choices: suggest that screening becomes unnecessary as treatments improve
argue that lead-time bias disappears over time
explain why a long trial may yield findings that no longer describe current practice
show that death rates are more affected by treatment than survival rates are
criticize researchers for delaying publication of their results
questions.explanation:
The sentence gives a drawback of death-rate trials: they run long, so by publication, practice may have moved on. That is C.

A is not suggested; the author supports screening where mortality falls. B confuses two unrelated ideas. D is not claimed; both measures are affected by treatment. E blames researchers, but the delay arises from the need for long follow-up, not carelessness.
questions.tip: A clause starting "and by the time" almost always states a consequence of the preceding limitation.
questions.trap: Answers that compare how treatment affects the two measures add a comparison the author never makes.

questions.prompt: Suppose a screening programme detects many slow-growing tumours that would never have harmed the patients, does not change the age at which any patient dies of the disease, and leads to treatment complications that cause a few deaths recorded under other headings. Based on the passage, which of the following is most likely to be true of this programme?
choices: Death rates from the disease would fall markedly in the screened population
Five-year survival rates would be unchanged, because lead-time bias and overdiagnosis would cancel each other
Five-year survival rates would fall, because slow-growing tumours rarely cause death
Five-year survival rates would look better in the screened group even though the programme's net effect on deaths would be zero or negative
Both five-year survival rates and disease-specific death rates would show a clear benefit
questions.explanation:
Overdiagnosis adds harmless cases to the "survivor" count, and earlier detection adds lead time, so five-year survival would rise. Because the age of death from the disease is unchanged, the disease-specific death rate would not fall, and complications recorded under other headings mean net deaths could even rise. That is D.

A contradicts the stipulation that no one dies later of the disease. B is wrong because both distortions push survival in the same direction (up), so they do not cancel. C reverses the effect of overdiagnosis. E claims a death-rate benefit that the scenario rules out.
questions.tip: In application questions, translate the scenario into the passage's named mechanisms (here, lead time, overdiagnosis, hidden complications) and ask which way each pushes each measure.
questions.trap: Assuming the two biases offset one another, when both inflate survival.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that bilingual education should be removed from school policy
describe how evidence about a claimed cognitive benefit has changed and weigh responses to the change
explain why executive functions are important to planning and self-control
show that publication bias is the sole cause of the early findings
compare the tasks used to measure executive function in different studies
questions.explanation:
The passage moves from early claims to weaker later evidence, then sets out the defenders' and sceptics' responses and a fair verdict. That is B.

A is a policy conclusion the author never draws. C is background, not the purpose. D overstates; the author says only that bias "may" have skewed the literature. E is one part of the defenders' reply, not the passage's aim.
questions.tip: "Describe a change and weigh responses" is the typical purpose of a passage that has a before, an after, and a verdict.
questions.trap: "Sole cause" claims overstate a hedged "may have".

questions.prompt: The author mentions the likelihood that studies reporting an advantage would appear in journals in order to
choices: give a reason for suspecting that the early literature overstated the benefit
prove that the early studies were conducted dishonestly
explain why large studies found no difference between bilingual and monolingual children
show that studies with no effect were never carried out
support the defenders' claim that the effect appears only for some tasks
questions.explanation:
The review is cited to show the early literature "may have been skewed by what got published": A.

B is too strong; publication bias is not dishonesty. C is not what the passage says; the large studies found no difference for their own reasons, not because of bias. D contradicts the passage, which refers to studies reporting no effect. E belongs to the defenders' reply, not to the point about publication.
questions.tip: A "review noted" sentence in an evaluative passage usually serves as a reason for doubt.
questions.trap: Jumping from "skewed" to "dishonest", which no sentence supports.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following studies would most likely help settle the dispute?
choices: A large study that compares all bilingual and monolingual children on a wide range of tasks and reports whichever differences emerge
A review of published studies that counts how many report a bilingual advantage
A survey of parents about whether their bilingual children seem better at planning
A study of bilingual children that selects the tasks on which earlier studies found an advantage and reports only those tasks
A study that states, before any data are collected, which children and which tasks should show the effect
questions.explanation:
The author ends by saying the question will need studies that "specify in advance which children and which tasks should show the effect." That is E.

A repeats the broad design that produced the null results and lets differences be explained after the fact. B reproduces the publication-count approach, which cannot test the hypothesis directly. C is a subjective impression, not a measure of executive function. D chooses tasks after seeing results, the very practice the sceptics object to.
questions.tip: The final sentence of an evaluative passage often states exactly what the better evidence would look like.
questions.trap: Selecting the study that reports only the favourable tasks, which is the post-hoc narrowing the passage warns against.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that online marketplaces should be exempt from rules against predatory pricing
explain how an online marketplace recovers its costs from sellers
recommend a single numerical test that regulators can use to identify predatory pricing
explain why a conventional test for predatory pricing fits two-sided platforms poorly and consider the difficulties of alternatives
compare the pricing strategies of mature and new platforms
questions.explanation:
The passage states the conventional test, explains why it fails for platforms, discusses the whole-platform alternative and its difficulties, and ends by saying a bright-line rule is of little use. That is D.

A is contradicted: "The upshot is not that platform pricing should be exempt from scrutiny." B describes only an example. C is the opposite of the final paragraph, which says regulators wanting a simple number "will be disappointed." E is a supporting detail in paragraph three.
questions.tip: Use the last paragraph's "the upshot" sentence as a check on any purpose choice.
questions.trap: Choosing the exemption answer, which is the very conclusion the author denies.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, a marketplace may let shoppers browse without charge because
choices: the presence of shoppers is what makes the platform valuable to the sellers who pay it
shoppers are less numerous than sellers and so cost less to serve
predatory pricing is permitted when the platform serves two groups
shoppers contribute a larger share of shared costs than sellers do
competition authorities require platforms to subsidise consumers
questions.explanation:
The passage says "it is the shoppers' presence that makes the platform worth paying for," which is A.

B reverses the passage; it never says shoppers are fewer. C states a legal conclusion the author does not make. D is unsupported; the passage says shared costs are allocated arbitrarily. E brings in a regulatory requirement that the passage never mentions.
questions.tip: The answer to a "because" detail question is often a restated phrase from the sentence right after the example.
questions.trap: Answers that sound economic ("cost less to serve") but have no textual basis.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that shared costs "can be allocated between the two sides only in a largely arbitrary way" primarily in order to
choices: show that platforms charge the two sides unfairly
argue that servers and engineers are more costly than other inputs
explain why assessing a platform as a whole is not a mechanical exercise either
suggest that predatory pricing is impossible to prove in court
support the claim that mature platforms are less harmful than new ones
questions.explanation:
The sentence is a difficulty listed against the whole-platform approach, which "has difficulties of its own." Arbitrary cost allocation means the assessment requires judgment: C.

A is about regulators' tests, not fairness to customers. B says nothing about how large these costs are. D goes further than the passage, which says only that the whole-platform approach is difficult. E concerns the age of a platform, a separate point.
questions.tip: Identify which paragraph-level claim a quoted phrase is serving ("has difficulties of its own") before choosing.
questions.trap: Taking an accounting problem and turning it into a legal or moral conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a situation warranting closer scrutiny for possible predatory pricing?
choices: A mature marketplace that has charged shoppers nothing for many years, with a seller commission that covers its total costs
A newly launched marketplace in a market with no established rival offers free service to one group and signs those users to exclusive long-term contracts
A platform whose revenue from one side is below its costs on that side, but whose total revenue exceeds its total costs
A retailer selling a single product at a loss for one week to clear unwanted inventory
A platform that explains its losses on one side as an investment in network effects
questions.explanation:
The author warns that in a new market, "subsidised users can be locked in before a rival has had the chance to reach the scale it needs." A new platform subsidising one side while locking users in matches that: B.

A describes a mature, self-sustaining platform, which the author treats as benign. C is the case that the whole-platform assessment would clear. D is a one-off promotion by a single-product seller. E is an explanation the author notes can be a disguise, but the explanation alone is not enough to flag a problem; the passage asks for an empirical test.
questions.tip: For "most likely warrants scrutiny" questions, find the conditions the author names as harmful and match all of them.
questions.trap: Picking the answer that merely repeats a phrase the author treats with suspicion, without the lock-in and new-market conditions.

questions.prompt: The passage as a whole is primarily concerned with
choices: arguing that automated vehicles are less safe than human drivers
showing why a seemingly simple standard for approving automated vehicles is hard to apply and suggesting a way forward
describing how companies measure the number of minor incidents in test fleets
proposing that automated vehicles be required to match the safest human drivers
explaining why fatal crashes are rare among human drivers
questions.explanation:
The author starts with a simple standard (safer than humans), shows two problems (measurement, comparison), notes the cost of a stricter standard, and proposes staged deployment. That is B.

A is contradicted; the author never claims the machines are worse. C is only a detail about indirect evidence. D is one view the author reports and then qualifies. E is not explained and is only a premise.
