questions.tip: If the passage ends by recommending a course of action, the purpose usually includes "and suggest".
questions.trap: Choosing the stricter benchmark, which the author presents as a view that carries its own cost.

questions.prompt: The passage states that test miles driven by automated systems differ from the miles driven by the average human driver in that they
choices: have been driven mostly by drivers who were sober and alert
have caused fewer minor incidents per mile
were driven at higher speeds on a wider range of roads
included a larger share of night driving
have mostly been driven in favourable conditions with a safety driver available to intervene
questions.explanation:
The third paragraph says test miles were "mostly driven in good weather, on carefully mapped roads, and with a safety driver ready to intervene." That is E.

A mixes up the human average with the test fleet. B is not stated; incident frequency is described as indirect evidence only. C contradicts the passage, which says the roads were carefully mapped. D is not mentioned.
questions.tip: For "differ in that" questions, locate the comparison sentence and confirm which group each clause describes.
questions.trap: Attributing a quality of the human average (including sober drivers) to the test fleet.

questions.prompt: The author mentions "drunk, drowsy, and distracted drivers" primarily in order to
choices: argue that automated vehicles should not be permitted to share roads with human drivers
show that most fatal crashes are caused by impaired drivers
support the claim that careful drivers are very rare
indicate that the human average may be a lenient benchmark for judging an automated system
suggest that the fatal crash rate of human drivers is higher than commonly reported
questions.explanation:
The phrase explains why the human average includes unusually dangerous drivers, so beating that average may be easier than beating a careful driver. That is D.

A is not argued. B is a statistic the passage does not give. C is unsupported; the passage does not say careful drivers are rare. E is not suggested either; the one-in-hundred-million figure is given without challenge.
questions.tip: Ask what conclusion the list is meant to support; here it is "the average is a low bar".
questions.trap: Choosing a factual claim about crash causes that the passage never makes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage about requiring automated vehicles to match a careful driver?
choices: It could, in some circumstances, lead to more deaths than a less demanding standard would
It would eliminate the problem of measuring fatal crashes
It is a standard that no automated system could ever meet
It is endorsed by the author as the most reasonable benchmark
It would make staged deployment unnecessary
questions.explanation:
The final paragraph says holding back a system that is safer than the average but not the best would leave the average driver on the road, "with all the deaths that implies." So the stricter standard might cost lives: A.

B is wrong because measurement is a separate problem that remains. C is too strong; the passage does not say it could never be met. D is wrong because the author says "no single benchmark can settle the matter." E reverses the author's view; staged deployment is recommended.
questions.tip: Inference answers often take the form "in some circumstances X could happen"; extreme versions fail.
questions.trap: Treating a view the author reports, the careful-driver standard, as the author's own recommendation.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that old paintings should never be cleaned
defend conservators against the charge that they damage paintings
distinguish the factual and evaluative elements in a dispute over the cleaning of old paintings
explain how modern solvent tests allow conservators to clean paintings safely
show that public alarm at cleaned paintings is based on ignorance of the artists' intentions
questions.explanation:
The author presents the critics, then the conservators, and then states that the dispute is "partly about facts and partly about values," explaining which elements analysis can settle. That is C.

A is the critics' extreme position, which the author does not adopt. B is too one-sided; the author also says conservators sometimes fail to respect the aged tone. D is a detail from the conservators' reply. E misrepresents the author, who gives the public's attachment to the aged tone some weight.
questions.tip: When the closing paragraph starts "partly... and partly...", the purpose is to separate two kinds of question.
questions.trap: Siding with the conservators because their paragraph contains the most technical detail.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, conservators defend the removal of old varnish on the grounds that
choices: viewers eventually come to prefer the brighter colours
varnish layers contain pigments that the artist applied to model shadows
public alarm at cleaned paintings is temporary
earlier generations of conservators were careless about glazes
the varnish was not part of the original work and was expected to be replaced when it darkened
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph says the varnish "was applied to protect the paint and was always expected to be replaced once it darkened." That is E.

A is not claimed by anyone in the passage. B reverses the point; glazes are paint, and varnish is a protective layer. C is not stated. D is partly implied by "greater precision than earlier generations," but it is not the ground on which conservators defend removal; it explains how, not why.
questions.tip: In "on the grounds that" questions, choose the stated reason, not the supporting method or side remark.
questions.trap: The earlier-generations choice borrows a phrase from the same paragraph but answers a different question.

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward the conservators' position is best described as
choices: respectful of their technical claims but unconvinced that they give enough weight to the value of the aged appearance
doubtful of their technical claims but sympathetic to their view of the artist's intentions
dismissive of their position as an attempt to avoid public criticism
neutral, offering no view beyond reporting what both sides say
approving of their position and critical of the critics' attachment to the aged tone
questions.explanation:
The author treats the factual question as decidable by sample analysis (consistent with the conservators' technical claim) but says the aged-tone claim "deserves more respect than conservators sometimes allow." That mixed attitude is A.

B reverses the author's stance on the technical claims; they are not doubted. C is unsupported; the author does not suggest bad faith. D is wrong because the final sentence takes a side on one question. E is wrong because the author does not criticise the critics' attachment; the author says it deserves respect.
questions.tip: Attitude questions are easiest when the author gives a split verdict; name the part approved and the part criticised.
questions.trap: The "neutral" option is tempting because the passage is balanced in structure, but the last sentence takes a stand.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: defend the claim that language determines thought
show that speakers of different languages cannot understand one another
criticize researchers who study colour perception
argue that Russian speakers perceive blue differently from English speakers
assess the evidence for a modest version of the claim that language influences perception, after setting aside a strong version
questions.explanation:
The first paragraph sets aside the strong claim, the second gives experimental evidence for a weaker one, the third handles objections, and the conclusion is "modest." That is E.

A is the strong form, which has "few defenders." B is not argued; the passage discusses incommensurable worlds only as a rejected idea. C is unsupported; the researchers' findings are used. D overstates; the author says language does not "alter the visual experience itself".
questions.tip: A passage that starts by dismissing a strong claim and ends with "modest" is assessing a weaker version.
questions.trap: The "differently" choice states the experimental result too strongly and ignores the author's qualification.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the advantage that Russian speakers show in distinguishing two shades of blue disappears when
choices: the shades fall on the same side of the lexical boundary
English speakers are given new words for the shades
participants repeat a string of digits while making their judgements
the experiment is conducted in a different laboratory
the shades are named aloud before the comparison
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph says "The effect vanishes, however, when participants are asked to repeat a string of digits while they work." That is C.

A is the condition under which the advantage does not arise at all, rather than a case of it vanishing. B is not tested in the passage. D concerns replication difficulty, a different matter from the digit task. E is never mentioned.
questions.tip: For a "when" detail question, find the exact trigger phrase; look for "however" or "but".
questions.trap: Choosing the condition where the effect never appears instead of the condition that removes it.

questions.prompt: The author mentions the digit-repetition result in the last sentence of the third paragraph primarily in order to
choices: concede that the experimental findings are difficult to replicate
show that Russian speakers have better memory for digits than English speakers
argue that experiences of different cultures are largely identical
support the view that the difference depends on verbal processing rather than on perceptual experience
suggest that language determines how people see colours
questions.explanation:
The author argues the second objection is "less damaging than it seems" because the effect disappears when the verbal system is occupied, even though perceptual experience is unchanged. That supports the verbal-processing explanation: D.

A is the first objection, which the author concedes separately. B is not claimed. C is irrelevant; the objection concerns differences in experience, which the author does not call identical. E contradicts the author's stance that language does not alter visual experience.
questions.tip: Link an example to the specific objection it answers; the sentence introducing it names the objection.
questions.trap: Choosing the "determines how people see" answer, which restores the strong claim the author rejected.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's response to the second objection?
choices: English speakers who were taught the Russian words for light and dark blue became faster at distinguishing those shades
Russian speakers who moved to English-speaking countries gradually lost their advantage
The digit-repetition task slowed every participant's judgements so much that any difference between the language groups would have been impossible to detect, whatever its source
The advantage for Russian speakers has been detected in several independent laboratories
Russian speakers on average report seeing blue objects more often than English speakers do
questions.explanation:
The author argues that the vanishing effect shows the difference is verbal, not perceptual. If the digit task would hide any difference whatever its cause, the disappearance proves nothing about its source, so C undermines the response.

A supports a language effect and so helps the author. B is consistent with a vocabulary-based effect and does not touch the digit argument. D bears on the first objection (replication) and, if anything, supports the author. E supports the sceptics' claim that experience differs, but the author's reply is that the digit result is hard to explain by experience alone, and this fact does not remove that difficulty.
questions.tip: To weaken an argument that rests on one piece of evidence, attack what the evidence actually shows, not the conclusion.
questions.trap: Picking the evidence that supports the sceptics' objection, which the author has already acknowledged.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: show that a popular loyalty measure is worse than longer satisfaction surveys in every industry
consider a defence of a business metric whose claimed predictive advantage has not held up
recommend that firms abandon customer surveys in favour of a single question
explain how a single loyalty score is calculated from customer answers
argue that managers should pay less attention to forecasts of revenue growth
questions.explanation:
The first paragraph says the predictive claim has mostly failed, and the second offers a plausible defence of the measure based on how it is used, while noting that this has not been tested. That is B.

A is too strong; the score is said to be worse only "in several industries," and the author says it is not useless. C is not recommended; the author says the single question may help. D is not described in the passage. E is never argued.
questions.tip: When the second paragraph begins "It would be a mistake, however," the passage is a defence-with-caveats, not an attack.
questions.trap: Answers with "every" or "abandon" overstate a hedged evaluation.

questions.prompt: The author mentions a "sixty-page report" most likely in order to
choices: criticize managers for failing to read long documents
suggest that longer surveys are less accurate than a single question
indicate that reports of that length are rarely produced
illustrate how the findings of longer surveys can fail to prompt action
argue that frontline staff dislike detailed data
questions.explanation:
The phrase appears in the defenders' argument that a single number is "hard to bury in a sixty-page report," and the next clause says managers had "ignored the findings of earlier surveys." The report illustrates how long surveys can fail to prompt action: D.

A puts blame on managers, which the passage does not do. B confuses usability with accuracy. C is not suggested. E overreaches; staff are said to find a single number easy to understand, not to dislike detail.
questions.tip: An odd specific detail (a number, a length) in a function question usually serves a contrast in the surrounding sentence.
questions.trap: Confusing a claim about use (action) with a claim about accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which of the following studies would best test the defenders' suggestion described in the second paragraph?
choices: A comparison of customer outcomes at firms that adopt the single score with outcomes at similar firms that adopt an equally simple but less predictive measure
A comparison of the single score's predictive power with that of longer surveys in additional industries
A survey of frontline staff asking whether they find the single score easy to understand
A comparison of firms that adopt the single score with firms that keep their longer surveys
An examination of the industries in which the single score predicted growth worst
questions.explanation:
The author states the needed design: compare firms that adopt the simple score with similar firms that adopt "an equally simple but less predictive measure." If outcomes improve equally, use rather than predictive accuracy matters. That is A.

B tests the predictive claim, which has already been examined. C measures the premise (ease of understanding) but not the effect on outcomes. D mixes simplicity with predictive power, so any difference could come from either. E examines the failed claim, not the defence.
questions.tip: A good test isolates one variable; here it is "simple and predictive" versus "simple but less predictive".
questions.trap: The option that compares simple with long surveys confounds two differences at once.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that vitamin D has no effect on health
criticize physicians for recommending supplements to the general public
describe how randomized trials are designed
explain why evidence on vitamin D supplements appears inconsistent and indicate what the evidence does and does not show
compare the effects of vitamin D on heart disease, diabetes, and cancer
questions.explanation:
The passage presents the conflict between observational and trial evidence, explains it, and then states the limits of the trials: no support for routine use, but the question about deficiency stays open. That is D.

A is rejected in paragraph three ("hasty to conclude..."). B blames physicians, which the author never does. C is a detail in the opening paragraph. E is not undertaken; the diseases are mentioned only as examples.
questions.tip: A passage that ends with "The honest summary" is almost always evaluative; the purpose will mention what evidence does and does not show.
questions.trap: Choosing "no effect", which the author expressly calls hasty.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that "sick people spend less time in the sun" primarily in order to
choices: argue that sunlight is more important to health than supplements
suggest that vitamin D is harmful to chronically ill people
illustrate how illness could produce low vitamin D rather than low vitamin D producing illness
explain why trial participants were not deficient at the outset
show that the habits of healthy people are unrelated to vitamin D
questions.explanation:
The sentence gives a way the causal arrow could point backward: "Chronic illness can itself lower vitamin D." That is C.

A is not claimed. B is unsupported; vitamin D is not said to be harmful. D concerns the trial participants, a different paragraph and topic. E reverses the earlier sentence, which says healthy habits accompany high levels.
questions.tip: When a function question quotes an odd detail, look for the "marker rather than cause" structure: reverse causation.
questions.trap: Picking the answer that sounds medically plausible but fails to match the sentence's role in the argument.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the randomized trials described are poorly suited to answering which of the following questions?
choices: Whether people who exercise more have higher vitamin D levels
Whether supplements reduce the risk of heart disease in healthy adults
Whether observational studies can separate vitamin D from other habits
Whether healthy volunteers were assigned at random to the placebo group
Whether supplements benefit people who are truly deficient in vitamin D
questions.explanation:
The third paragraph says these trials mostly enrolled people with adequate levels and "cannot show that correcting a true deficiency is pointless." So they are poorly suited to the question in E.

A is outside what the trials tested; it concerns observational habits. B is the question the trials were well suited to answer. C is a general point about observational studies, not about the trials. D is also answered by the design (assignment by lot).
questions.tip: Limitations the author states for a method map directly onto the question the method cannot answer.
questions.trap: Choosing the question the trials answered best, because it is the one most discussed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's claim that the case for treating deficient people remains open?
choices: Most participants in the earlier trials were already taking vitamin D supplements on their own
A large trial restricted to deficient participants found no reduction in disease among those who took supplements
Chronic illness is a common cause of low vitamin D levels
Most adults in the general population have adequate vitamin D levels
Observational studies show that people with higher vitamin D levels exercise more
questions.explanation:
The author says the question of treating deficiency is open because few trials have studied deficient people. A large trial of deficient people showing no benefit would answer the question against supplements, weakening the claim: B.

A supports the author's point that the earlier trials were poorly suited to the question. C repeats an explanation already given in the passage. D is consistent with the claim that routine supplementation for the public is unsupported. E restates the confounding point and has no bearing on deficiency.
questions.tip: To weaken "the question remains open", supply an answer to the question.
questions.trap: Picking facts that merely repeat the passage's confounding explanation.

questions.prompt: The main point of the passage is that
choices: dynamic pricing should be abandoned because customers dislike it
customers who object to surge pricing do not understand how markets work
although dynamic pricing has real economic advantages, customers' sense of fairness is a genuine consideration that firms should manage
fixed prices always produce longer waits than dynamic prices
caps on price multipliers have been proved to restore customer trust
questions.explanation:
The first paragraph gives the economic case, the second explains why customers' reaction is not irrational, and the third recommends managing fairness. That is C.

A is rejected: "None of this means that firms should abandon dynamic pricing." B is the view the author calls "too quick." D is too strong; the author says only that a fixed price leaves the market short of drivers when they are needed. E is wrong because the passage says whether these measures suffice "remains an open question."
questions.tip: When a passage says "That dismissal is too quick", the author's main point sits between the two sides.
questions.trap: Choosing the "proved" option, which contradicts the author's caution about short experiments.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, customers are most likely to accept a price increase when it
choices: occurs during bad weather
is announced after the service has been provided
is applied equally by all competing firms
is smaller than the increase in the customer's urgency
tracks a rise in the firm's costs
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph says people "accept price increases that track a firm's costs but resent increases that merely exploit their lack of alternatives." That is E.

A is the example of a situation people resent, since weather raises urgency, not cost. B is not mentioned; the passage speaks of showing the price before confirmation. C is not discussed. D describes the very opportunism that provokes resentment.
questions.tip: For acceptance/resentment questions, locate the contrast sentence ("accept... but resent") and take the accepted half.
questions.trap: Choosing the rainy-evening case, which is the passage's example of what customers resent.

questions.prompt: The author mentions presenting off-peak fares as discounts in order to
choices: give an example of a reframing that leaves the economics unchanged but may reduce resentment
show that discounts are more profitable than surcharges
argue that customers cannot tell the difference between a discount and a surcharge
suggest that peak prices should be eliminated
illustrate how a fixed price leaves a market short of supply
questions.explanation:
The author calls this "a reframing that leaves the economics unchanged yet appears to reduce resentment." That is A.

B is wrong because the author says the economics are unchanged, so profit is not the point. C is the opposite: the customers' reaction differs, so they do see a difference. D is not suggested; peak pricing continues in the reframing. E belongs to the first paragraph and is unrelated.
questions.tip: When a function question gives an example inside a list, the author's own gloss after the list usually states its purpose.
questions.trap: Reading "leaves the economics unchanged" as a claim about profitability.

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that a competitor offering a predictable fare structure could
choices: avoid shortages of drivers at times of peak demand
earn higher profits than a surge-pricing platform in the long run
prevent customers from feeling that fares are unfair
attract some customers from a surge-pricing platform even though it responds more slowly to demand
persuade economists that fixed prices are better than dynamic prices
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph says exploited customers "may switch to a competitor with a more predictable fare structure, even if that competitor is slower to respond to changes in demand." That is D.

A is contradicted by the first paragraph, which says fixed prices leave a shortage when demand spikes. B is not claimed; the passage speaks of customers switching, not profits. C is too strong; the passage says only that fairness resentment would be reduced for surge pricing. E is not suggested; economists are said to approve of surge pricing.
questions.tip: "Could" inference choices should restate a possibility the passage mentions, not a guarantee.
questions.trap: The profit answer extends a customer-switching statement into a profitability claim.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that the sharing of meat among foragers is motivated entirely by self-interest
compare several explanations of a social practice and suggest that a combination of them is needed
show that signalling is the most widely accepted explanation of food-sharing
describe the techniques by which foragers hunt large game
prove that tolerated theft cannot explain any case of food-sharing
questions.explanation:
The passage sets out three explanations, notes strengths and weaknesses of each, and concludes that a satisfactory account "probably has to combine" insurance and group norms. That is B.

A describes only the reciprocity account, which the author qualifies. C is contradicted by the evidence being described as "mixed". D is not the subject; hunting is mentioned only as context. E is too strong; the author says tolerated theft captures "something real".
questions.tip: Count the views and look at how the last paragraph treats them; if it says "none alone", the purpose is comparative.
questions.trap: "Prove...cannot explain any case" overstates a limited criticism.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is a weakness of the signalling account?
choices: It cannot explain why large animals are hunted at all
It assumes that hunters never receive any reward for sharing
It predicts that stingy hunters will be shunned
It does not readily account for the fact that meat is often distributed by someone other than the hunter
It cannot explain why good hunters have more partners
questions.explanation:
The third paragraph says the theory "struggles to explain why the meat is frequently distributed by someone other than the hunter." That is D.

A is not claimed. B reverses the account, which says hunters gain status. C is a point about tolerated theft, not signalling. E is the reverse; the passage says good hunters do enjoy more partners, which supports signalling.
questions.tip: For "weakness of X" questions, find the sentence that begins with "but" or "struggles" inside X's own paragraph.
questions.trap: Choosing a detail from the neighbouring account that sounds like a weakness.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author regards the sharing of honey as
choices: evidence that foragers value honey more than meat
strong support for the reciprocity account
proof that foragers share only out of generosity
evidence that signalling plays no role in foraging societies
a case that tolerated theft cannot explain on its own
questions.explanation:
The author notes that the theory predicts sharing should be strongest for resources that cannot be hidden, "but the sharing of easily concealed items such as honey has often been reported to follow similar rules." So honey is a hard case for tolerated theft by itself: E.

A compares values, which the passage does not discuss. B is wrong because reciprocity is criticised on a different point (proportionality). C is too strong; the author does not say sharing is purely generous. D is too strong as well; signalling is said to have mixed evidence, not none.
questions.tip: Tie each piece of evidence to the specific prediction it tests; honey tests the hiding prediction.
questions.trap: Treating any example given as support for the account named in the same paragraph.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's criticism of the reciprocity account?
choices: Hunters who are slow to hand over meat are teased by other members of the camp
Good hunters enjoy extra status and more partners than other members of the camp
Households that contributed almost no meat in recent seasons received nearly as much meat as households that contributed the most
Large game is caught rarely and unpredictably
Honey, which can be hidden, is shared according to rules similar to those for meat
questions.explanation:
The author criticises reciprocity because sharing "is only weakly related to past contributions." Households that gave little yet received nearly as much further weaken the link between giving and receiving: C.

A supports tolerated theft. B supports signalling. D is a premise of the reciprocity account (rarity of large game), not a criticism of it. E bears on tolerated theft, which predicts sharing to be strongest for what can't be hidden.
questions.tip: Match the new evidence to the specific prediction the author says the account fails.
questions.trap: Choosing a fact that damages a different account named in the passage.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: prove that readers' emotions in response to fiction are not genuine
argue that daydreaming is as emotionally powerful as reading a novel
explain why readers do not call the police when a fictional character is murdered
present a puzzle about emotional responses to fiction and compare two proposed solutions, each of which faces a difficulty
describe the physiological changes that accompany strong emotion
questions.explanation:
The passage states the puzzle, gives the quasi-emotion solution with its cost, gives the rival view with its difficulty, and ends with a suggestion. That is D.

A is the first response, which the author criticises. B is wrong because the passage says few readers would say a daydream moves them as a novel does. C is a supporting example in the first paragraph. E is a detail, used as evidence against the first response.
questions.tip: In puzzle-and-solutions passages, the purpose is to compare, and each solution usually gets its "however".
questions.trap: Selecting a detail used as evidence instead of the passage's overall aim.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that readers' "hearts do race" most likely in order to
choices: provide evidence against the claim that readers' reactions are merely make-believe
show that readers cannot distinguish fiction from reality
support the claim that real pity requires a belief in the sufferer's reality
suggest that vivid memories of danger cause physical reactions
argue that novels move readers more than films do
questions.explanation:
The sentence follows "The response has a cost" and says readers' reactions are "physiologically indistinguishable" from reactions to a real tragedy, which counts against calling them make-believe: A.

B goes too far; readers know the characters are invented. C is the assumption that the author is questioning. D is a different example, offered later for the rival view. E is not discussed; films are never mentioned.
questions.tip: The sentence just before a detail often says what the detail is for ("The response has a cost").
questions.trap: Picking an answer that fits the topic but not the argumentative role of the detail.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most support the rival view described in the second paragraph?
choices: People who watch fictional crimes seldom report them to the police
Readers who are moved by novels are no more likely than others to donate to charity
People who vividly imagine themselves in a dangerous situation show physical signs of fear even though they know they are safe
Most readers find it easier to weep at a film than at a novel
Readers can usually remember the names of characters who die in novels
questions.explanation:
The rival view says emotions can be prompted by vividly imagined situations even without belief. People who show fear while knowing they are safe are an instance: C.

A is consistent with both views, since neither predicts action. B concerns charity, which neither view addresses directly. D compares media, which is irrelevant. E says only that readers remember names.
questions.tip: To support a view, find evidence that matches its specific claim (emotion without belief).
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about lack of action, which both views already explain.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: demonstrate that electric cars are always cleaner than petrol cars
argue that the manufacture of batteries makes electric cars dirtier than petrol cars
describe how life-cycle analyses are conducted
recommend that electric cars with very large batteries be discouraged
argue that the environmental advantage of electric cars depends on conditions that vary, and point to a factor that both sides underplay
questions.explanation:
The passage reports the sceptics, the life-cycle analyses, and the critics' reply, then says the answer depends on grid, battery size and mileage and adds that both sides neglect the changing grid. That is E.

A is contradicted by the unfavourable cases in paragraph two and three. B is the sceptics' position, which the author says is only partly right. C is a detail in paragraph two. D is a conclusion only about very large batteries in lightly used vehicles, not the whole passage.
questions.tip: "Both sides are, in a sense, right" signals a reframing purpose: conditions matter.
questions.trap: Choosing an "always" or "dirtier" answer, which takes one side.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the critics of life-cycle analyses claim that such analyses
choices: ignore the manufacture of batteries
tend to assume average driving distances and average electricity grids
overestimate the lifetime of electric cars
fail to count emissions from petrol cars
assume that the electricity grid will not change
questions.explanation:
The second paragraph says critics reply that "such studies tend to assume average driving distances and average electricity grids." That is B.

A is wrong; the analyses add up emissions from manufacture. C is not stated. D is not stated either; the analyses compare electric cars against petrol cars. E is the author's own point about the grid, not the critics'.
questions.tip: Attribute claims to the right party: "critics reply" sentences are the answer source.
questions.trap: Choosing the author's own point (changing grid) as if the critics had made it.

questions.prompt: The author mentions that an electric car bought today "will be charged for a decade or more" most likely in order to
choices: argue that electric cars last longer than petrol cars
show that batteries must be replaced after ten years
introduce the point that the grid's emissions are likely to change during the car's use
suggest that critics have underestimated the cost of charging
support the claim that the break-even point arrives within two years
questions.explanation:
The sentence continues, "during which the grid in most countries is expected to draw on a growing share of lower-emission generation." The decade is introduced to show the grid will change while the car is in use: C.

A is not claimed. B is not mentioned. D concerns cost, which the passage does not discuss. E is unrelated; the two-year figure refers to favourable conditions.
questions.tip: When a time span is mentioned, ask what changes over it; the following clause tells you.
questions.trap: Reading the "decade" as a claim about car lifetimes rather than about the grid.

questions.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's claim that the changing grid shifts the balance toward electric cars?
choices: In most countries, the share of coal-fired generation in the electricity supply has been rising and is forecast to keep rising
The emissions per kilometre of a petrol car are expected to stay roughly constant over its lifetime
Electric cars bought today are usually kept by their first owners for more than ten years
Very large batteries add more to manufacturing emissions than small batteries do
Under favourable conditions, an electric car recoups its manufacturing emissions within two years
questions.explanation:
The author's claim depends on the grid drawing on "a growing share of lower-emission generation." If coal's share is rising instead, the grid would get dirtier and the balance would not shift toward electric cars: A.

B is already stated in the passage and supports the claim. C supports the claim by lengthening the time over which the grid can change. D is consistent with the passage and does not touch the grid forecast. E restates the favourable case.
questions.tip: To weaken a claim built on a forecast, show that the forecast may point the other way.
questions.trap: Choosing a fact the passage already contains, which cannot be new damage.
